gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Marshall's US page sells the Emberton III ($179.99 on 2026-11-08) as 'Bluetooth LE Audio-ready' only 'once there are source devices on the market', with Auracast still a future feature and no codecs or aux input listed, so with a TV it works only as a classic Bluetooth speaker.
standout_why: I compared against geekchamp.com/bluetooth-tv-speakers-5-soundbars-that-make-tv-audio-better (rank 3/4 in both chats), which already covers most of this angle in general terms. It says aptX Low Latency or Adaptive cuts lag to about 40–50 ms 'only when both transmitter and speaker support the same codec' (citing PCWorld). It lists the 1Mii B06TX transmitter's optical, 3.5 mm and RCA inputs. It notes the Sony HT-S100F 'ships with optical rather than HDMI'. It also says Bluetooth from the TV is 'the least reliable option'. What it lacks is a model-by-model table: which named speaker accepts which codec from which TV or transmitter. It names no codecs for any pick, and it never mentions the Marshall Emberton III or the Bose SoundLink Flex (2nd Gen). I could not open itechguides.com (the page ChatGPT cited: timeout) or whathifi.com best soundbars (the cited page was truncated). So I can't rule out that one of them covers a codec table.
decides: This confirms the pick rather than changing it. Both chats steer the shopper to a soundbar connected by HDMI ARC or optical, and nothing I found argues against that. For the shopper who wants 'Bluetooth only', my sources say no low-latency path is documented for the portable speakers here. Marshall's US page lists no codec for the Emberton III, so pairing it with an aptX Low Latency transmitter such as the 1Mii B06TX can't be shown to give the low-latency mode. That speaker should be offered for music or casual TV only, not lip-sync-critical viewing.
